samples.guide: Use familiar concrete words, explicit subjects, one idea per clause and clear repetition. Preserve noun capitalization, umlauts and ß. Use correct case, agreement and verb placement.
samples.brief: Two friends at a railway station discover their tickets are for different destinations.

content.title: Zwei Fahrkarten
content.story:
Mia und Ben sind am Bahnhof. Mia hat eine Tasche. Ben hat einen Rucksack. Die Freunde wollen zusammen nach Bonn fahren.

Ein Zug steht am Gleis. Mia nimmt ihre Fahrkarte aus der Tasche.

„Unser Zug fährt nach Bonn“, sagt Mia. „Hast du deine Fahrkarte?“

„Ja“, sagt Ben. Er nimmt seine Fahrkarte aus dem Rucksack.

Mia schaut auf ihre Fahrkarte.

„Hier steht Bonn“, sagt sie.

Ben schaut auf seine Fahrkarte. Er liest: „Berlin.“

„Fährst du nach Berlin?“, fragt Mia.

„Nein. Ich möchte mit dir nach Bonn fahren.“

Ben zeigt Mia seine Fahrkarte. Mia liest den Namen der Stadt.

„Ja, hier steht Berlin. Deine Fahrkarte ist für Berlin. Meine Fahrkarte ist für Bonn.“

Ben schaut auf die zwei Fahrkarten.

„Oh“, sagt er. „Wir haben Fahrkarten für zwei verschiedene Städte.“

„Ja“, sagt Mia. „Wir können so nicht zusammen fahren.“

Neben dem Gleis ist ein Schalter. Ein Mann sitzt dort.

Ben steckt seine Fahrkarte nicht zurück in den Rucksack.

„Wir brauchen Hilfe“, sagt er.

Mia nickt. Die Freunde gehen mit ihren Fahrkarten zum Schalter.

glossary.meaning: railway station; “am Bahnhof” means “at the railway station”
ticket for a train or other public transport
train
to; used before city names to indicate a destination
different; here, the tickets are for two different cities
railway track; “am Gleis” means “by the track”
service counter, where the friends can ask for help
together
to need; “Wir brauchen Hilfe” means “We need help”
“Are you travelling …?” In this yes/no question, the verb comes before the subject.

content.title: Zwei Fahrkarten
content.story:
Mia und Paul stehen am Bahnhof. Mia hat eine Tasche. Paul hat einen Rucksack. Sie wollen zusammen nach Berlin fahren.

„Hast du deine Fahrkarte?“, fragt Mia.

„Ja, hier“, sagt Paul. Er nimmt die Fahrkarte aus seinem Rucksack.

Mia sieht auf ihre Fahrkarte.

„Mein Zug fährt nach Berlin“, sagt sie. „Wohin fährt dein Zug?“

Paul liest seine Fahrkarte.

„Mein Zug fährt nach Bremen.“

Er sieht Mia an.

„Nach Bremen? Ich will auch nach Berlin!“

„Zeig mir deine Fahrkarte“, sagt Mia.

Paul zeigt Mia die Fahrkarte. Mia hält ihre Fahrkarte daneben.

„Hier steht Berlin“, sagt Mia. „Und auf deiner Fahrkarte steht Bremen.“

Paul liest die Namen noch einmal.

„Die Stadt ist anders“, sagt er. „Meine Fahrkarte ist nicht für Berlin.“

„Ja“, sagt Mia. „Wir haben Fahrkarten für zwei verschiedene Städte.“

Paul sieht einen Schalter. Dort sitzt eine Frau.

„Wir brauchen Hilfe“, sagt er.

Mia nickt. Die beiden gehen mit ihren Fahrkarten zum Schalter.

glossary.meaning: And; joins people or statements.
To stand; stehen is the present-tense form used with Mia and Paul together.
At the; short for an dem. Here it gives the location at the station.
Railway station; Bahnhof follows am here.
To have; hat goes with one person, Hast with du in a question, and haben with wir.
A or an; eine is used with feminine nouns, and einen with masculine nouns as direct objects.
Bag.
Backpack.
They or she; Sie refers to both friends at the beginning, while sie later refers to Mia.
To want to; wollen is plural, while will goes with ich. The action verb fahren comes later in the clause.
Together.
To, before a city name; marks the destination of a journey.
To travel or go by transport; fährt means a train goes to a destination.
You, when speaking informally to one person.
Your, when addressing one person informally; dein goes with Zug, deine with Fahrkarte, and deiner follows auf for a location.
Travel ticket; Fahrkarten is plural.
To ask; fragt means Mia asks.
Yes; confirms or agrees with what someone says.
Here; points to the ticket or the writing on it.
To say; sagt is used with one speaker.
He; refers to Paul.
To take; nimmt means he takes the ticket out of his backpack.
The; die is used with feminine nouns and plural nouns in this story.
Out of; followed by the dative case in aus seinem Rucksack.
His; seinem refers to Paul's backpack after aus, and seine refers to his ticket as a direct object.
To look at something; Mia looks at her ticket.
Her or their; ihre means Mia's here, while ihren means the two friends' after mit.
My; Mein goes with the masculine noun Zug, and Meine with the feminine noun Fahrkarte.
Train.
Where to; asks about a destination rather than a current location.
To read; liest is the present-tense form for one person.
To look at someone; this separable verb places an after the person being looked at.
I; the speaker refers to himself.
Also or too; Paul also wants to go to Berlin.
To show; Zeig is an informal command to one person, and zeigt describes what Paul does.
To me; the dative form of ich identifies who should be shown the ticket.
To hold; hält means Mia holds her ticket beside Paul's.
Beside it; here, beside the other ticket.
To be written; steht tells which city name appears on a ticket, not where someone is standing.
On; auf deiner Fahrkarte means on your ticket. The ticket takes the dative case here.
Name; Namen is plural and refers to the city names printed on the tickets.
Once again; Paul reads the names another time.
City; Städte is the plural form, with an umlaut.
To be; ist is the present-tense form for one thing, such as the city or ticket.
Different; the city on Paul's ticket is not the same as Mia's destination.
Not; makes the statement negative.
For; identifies the destination for which a ticket is valid.
We; refers to Mia and Paul together.
Two.
Different; verschiedene describes the two cities as not being the same.
To see or notice; sieht means Paul notices a service counter.
Service or ticket counter at the station.
There; refers to the counter Paul has noticed.
To sit or be seated; sitzt describes the woman at the counter.
Woman.
To need; brauchen goes with wir here.
Help or assistance.
To nod; nickt means Mia nods in agreement.
The two of them; refers to Mia and Paul together.
To go or walk; gehen describes both friends walking to the counter.
With; followed by the dative case in mit ihren Fahrkarten.
To the; short for zu dem, used here for movement toward the counter.

materialIssues: “Ben steckt seine Fahrkarte nicht zurück in den Rucksack.” introduces a separable verb, negation and directional phrasing without support. This is a relatively demanding combination against the guide's simple-clause emphasis; the negative action also adds little to the scene.
“Wir können so nicht zusammen fahren.” combines a modal construction with the context-dependent meaning of “so” (‘with the tickets as they are’), neither of which is explained.
“Mia liest den Namen der Stadt.” contains a genitive noun phrase, “der Stadt”, that increases grammatical load beyond the otherwise very simple clauses.

“Hier steht Bonn” uses “steht” to mean ‘is written’, but this useful contextual sense is not explained. Broad support is also missing for many everyday words, contrary to the learner's explicit preference.
strengths: Correct case, agreement, verb placement, capitalization and umlauts throughout.
All supplied notes accurately explain their contextual meanings and listed forms.
Clear repetition makes the destination mismatch easy to follow.
The friends' move toward the counter provides a natural unresolved next step.

materialIssues: “Die Stadt ist anders” is grammatical but imprecise and less idiomatic here: the destination or printed city name differs, rather than the city itself being described as different.
“Mia sieht auf ihre Fahrkarte.” is understandable, but “schaut auf ihre Fahrkarte” would be a more ordinary choice in this scene. This is a naturalness preference, not a grammatical error.

“ansehen” is accurately translated, but the explanation “this separable verb places an after the person being looked at” is structurally imprecise. In this main clause, the separated prefix occupies the clause-final position; it is not generally placed immediately after the person.

“Zeig mir deine Fahrkarte” and “aus seinem Rucksack” introduce an imperative with a dative recipient and a dative possessive form. These increase beginner grammatical load, although the notes provide useful contextual support.
strengths: Broad definitions cover both common vocabulary and the scene's harder expressions without relying on note count alone.
Useful distinctions include physical “stehen” versus written “steht”, destination “wohin”, and the contextual possessive forms.
The possessive headword “sein” correctly means ‘his’ in its note; the separate verb entry correctly explains “ist”.
Correct grammar and orthography, clear ticket comparison, and a natural unresolved move toward help.

It explains written “steht”, possessive forms, “Zeig”, “mir” and “zum”, whereas sample-1 leaves several comparable constructions unsupported. Sample-2's minor wording and explanatory weaknesses do not outweigh that advantage.
